_comment: Every messaging service Ari can target by name. Adding one is a data
change, not a code change — which matters because this list is always
wrong somewhere: LINE in Japan, KakaoTalk in Korea, Zalo in Vietnam,
Viber across eastern Europe. A service missing from here still reaches
the user through the system share chooser; an entry just saves them
picking the app.
contact_mimetype is the row a service writes into ContactsContract when
it syncs the address book. id_column and the strip fields say where the
usable identifier lives inside that row — they differ per service, so
they are data rather than an assumption. Services with no mimetype can
still be targeted; they just can't have a recipient resolved.
url_template opens the recipient's chat with the message already typed —
one tap instead of picking a name. Both verified on device. The scheme
form is preferred over url_fallback because an https app-link falls
through to a browser install page when the app is absent. Both templates
want bare digits, which is why the Telegram prefix strips the + too.
can_send marks a service Ari can send itself, with nobody tapping
anything. Only SMS qualifies on Android: every other messenger keeps
sending to itself. It is also the only one that needs a confirmation,
because it is the only one where no human sees the message first.
An entry with no packages is addressed by scheme rather than by app —
email goes to whichever client the user has set as default, which is the
whole point of mailto:. Those entries need intent_action sendto.
contact_source says which standard contact field holds the address, for
services that use one instead of writing their own row.
